Read the three tables with the caution that Chapter 5 taught us: the test sets are small, and the intervals are wide.

Diabetes. Ridge (\alpha = 20), least squares and k-NN (k = 16) have test RMSE of 53.1, 53.4 and 54.5, against 74.9 for the baseline. The three intervals overlap almost completely, and the paired bootstrap interval for the difference between ridge and k-NN, [-5.1, 2.3], contains zero. With n = 331 training patients and p = 10 predictors, the gain of ridge over least squares is negligible, which is what the repeated-splits table of Section 6.3.4 predicted: at n = 331 the mean gain of ridge over least squares was a slight loss. All three beat the baseline by a wide margin: the predictors carry real information, and a linear relationship captures most of it.

Breast Cancer. The regularized logistic regression makes 5 errors and k-NN (k = 3) makes 6; the McNemar test (p = 1.0, with 4 and 3 discordant patients) cannot tell them apart, and the intervals for the accuracy, about [0.92, 0.99], overlap. The probabilities are another matter: the log-loss is 0.078 for the logistic model and 0.308 for k-NN, and the AUC is 0.996 against 0.988. k-NN gives probabilities that are multiples of 1/k and, when it is confidently wrong, pays heavily for them; the logistic model has smooth probabilities, trained for exactly this loss.

Digits. Here k-NN on the raw pixels is better, with 7 errors against 12, and this is the only comparison where the point estimates favor k-NN clearly. Even so, the McNemar test (3 against 8 discordant images, p = 0.23) does not reject the hypothesis that the two classifiers are equally accurate, in line with the intervals, which overlap. The linear model is the less accurate of the two and has the better log-loss (0.100 against 0.491).

The comparison illustrates the theme of the chapter. A linear model, regularized with a penalty chosen by validation, is a strong default: it is fast, it has few hyperparameters, it gives probabilities, and its performance is rarely far from that of the more flexible method. Whether a more flexible method can demonstrably do better depends on the problem and on the size of the data, and the evidence has to be gathered with the protocol of Chapter 5, not guessed from a single number.

Least squares. Under the linear model with noise variance \sigma^2, the OLS estimator is unbiased with covariance \sigma^2(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1} and is the best linear unbiased estimator (Gauss–Markov). With p parameters and n examples, the expected training error is \sigma^2(1 - p/n), the expected test error \sigma^2(1 + p/n), and \hat\sigma^2 = \mathrm{RSS}/(n - p) is unbiased. On Diabetes, \hat\sigma = 54.2 and R^2 = 0.52.

Computing it. The normal equations square the condition number: on a degree-9 polynomial basis, with \kappa(\mathbf{X}) = 3.6 \cdot 10^6, they lose about seven digits more than QR or SVD (error 2 \cdot 10^{-4} against 

10-10 or less), and at degree 12 they fail altogether. Use numpy.linalg.lstsq (SVD) or QR.

Collinearity. The variance of a coefficient is multiplied by the variance inflation factor \mathrm{VIF}_j = 1/(1 - R_j^2); on Diabetes the standard errors of the five blood-serum variables s1 to s5 are 8 to 20 against 3 for the others, and on Breast Cancer 23 of the 30 features have a VIF above 10 (above 3800 for mean radius). Individual coefficients become unreliable although the predictions stay good.

Ridge. \hat{\mathbf{w}}_\lambda = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X} + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{y} always exists, equals least squares on data augmented with \sqrt\lambda\,\mathbf{I}, and shrinks each singular direction by the factor \sigma_j^2/(\sigma_j^2 + \lambda): the low-variance directions, where the data are least informative, are shrunk most. Its effective number of parameters is \mathrm{df}(\lambda) = \sum_j\sigma_j^2/(\sigma_j^2 + \lambda), and the optimism of the training error is 2\sigma^2\,\mathrm{df}. Standardize the features and leave the intercept unpenalized.

Bias and variance, exactly. Ridge adds bias and removes variance; for small \lambda the variance saved is of first order and the bias added is of second order, so some \lambda > 0 always lowers the risk (Hoerl–Kennard), with \lambda^\ast = \sigma^2 d/\lVert\mathbf{w}^\ast\rVert^2 for an orthonormal design. In a simulated world on the real Diabetes design, the gain is 3.6% at n = 442 and 47.6% at n = 40: regularization matters when n is small relative to p and the signal is weak. On the real data it vanished at n_{\text{train}} = 331 (a mean gain of -10 on a test MSE of about 3000).

Choosing \lambda. The leave-one-out error of ridge is computed from one fit, \mathrm{LOO} = \frac1n\sum_i(e_i/(1 - h_{ii}))^2 (equal, to the last digit, to 331 refits), for all \lambda at once from the SVD. The LOO, 10-fold and test-optimal values of \lambda differ (1.6, 20, 63), but the validation curves are flat near their minima: the loss from a poor choice is small.

The three views. Penalty = constraint on the norm of the weights (the capacity control of Section 3.8, with \lambda the Lagrange multiplier) = Gaussian prior on the weights, with \lambda = \sigma^2/\tau^2.

Logistic regression models the log-odds as linear, \mathbb{P}(y = 1 \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b). Least squares on 0/1 labels leaves [0, 1] for 95 of the 569 Breast Cancer patients. The maximum-likelihood loss is the cross-entropy, convex, with gradient \tilde{\mathbf{X}}^\top(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{y}) and Hessian \tilde{\mathbf{X}}^\top\mathbf{S}\tilde{\mathbf{X}}, \mathbf{S} = \mathrm{diag}(p_i(1 - p_i)). Newton’s method is a sequence of weighted least-squares fits (IRLS) and converges quadratically: 8 iterations from \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0} on the 30 standardized features.

Separable data. If the classes can be separated there is no maximum-likelihood estimate: the weights diverge and the probabilities tend to 0 and 1. This happens on Iris (setosa against versicolor) and on the Breast Cancer training set; the unpenalized fit is determined by the stopping rule, and its test log-loss is 2.17 against 0.078 for C = 1.

Regularized logistic regression minimizes the mean log-loss +\ \frac\lambda2\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2, with \lambda = 1/(Cn) in scikit-learn’s parametrization (small C = strong regularization). It has a unique minimizer for every \lambda > 0. The cross-validated log-loss is U-shaped in C while the accuracy is almost flat over three decades: tune with the metric that measures what you need. With weak regularization the coefficients of collinear features take large values of opposite signs.

Softmax regression gives each of the K classes a linear score and normalizes with e^{z_k}/\sum_j e^{z_j}; the loss is the multi-class cross-entropy, the probabilities are invariant to adding the same vector to all the class weights, and the penalty selects the solution with \sum_k\mathbf{w}_k = \mathbf{0}. On Digits, test accuracy 0.973.

Feature maps. A model that is linear in \boldsymbol\varphi(\mathbf{x}) is nonlinear in \mathbf{x} and uses the same machinery. With p > n, ridge is still well defined and has a dual form, \hat{\mathbf{w}} = \mathbf{X}^\top(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{X}^\top + \lambda\mathbf{I})^{-1}\mathbf{y}, that involves only the inner products between training points (Chapter 9). On Diabetes with 100 training patients, polynomial features of degree 2 and 3 are disastrous without regularization (test MSE 18949 and 38221) and, with ridge, still worse than the linear model (3656 and 3766 against 3161); on two Breast Cancer features the degree-4 boundary with C = 1 is slightly better than the line, and the same polynomial with almost no penalty is much worse.

Against k-NN. On Diabetes, Breast Cancer and Digits the regularized linear models and k-NN are statistically indistinguishable in accuracy and RMSE (the confidence intervals overlap almost completely, the paired bootstrap interval for ridge against k-NN on Diabetes contains zero, and the McNemar p-values are 1.0 and 0.23); the linear models give much better probabilities (log-loss 0.078 against 0.308 on Breast Cancer).

Exercise 6.1 ★ — Variances by hand. A line y = b + wx is fitted by least squares to four points with x = -3, -1, 1, 3, and the noise has variance \sigma^2 = 4. Hint. For (a), \mathbf{p} = \tfrac12\mathbf{1} and \mathbf{S} = \tfrac14\mathbf{I} at the origin. For (b), L'(w) = -2\sigma(-w) and L''(w) = 2\sigma(w)\sigma(-w), and \sigma(-w)/(\sigma(w)\sigma(-w)) = 1/\sigma(w) = 1 + e^{-w}. For (c), J'(w) = -\sigma(-w) + \lambda w is strictly increasing.

Hint. The corrected statistic is t = \bar d\big/\sqrt{(1/J + n_{\text{test}}/n_{\text{train}})\,s_d^2} with J the number of splits, and J - 1 degrees of freedom. Use train_test_split(..., train_size=n_train, test_size=111, random_state=r).

Exercise 6.7 ★★ — Three ways to compute ridge, and GCV. (a) Write ridge_svd, ridge_aug (least squares on the augmented data) and ridge_normal (normal equations), each returning the intercept and the weights, for the standardized Diabetes training data of Section 6.3.1, and compare them with Ridge(alpha=10). (b) Plot \mathrm{df}(\lambda) for \lambda from 

10-2 to 

104. (c) Compute the generalized cross-validation score \mathrm{GCV}(\lambda) = n\,\mathrm{RSS}(\lambda)/(n - \mathrm{df}(\lambda))^2 and find its minimizer. Compare it with the minimizer of the leave-one-out curve of Section 6.3.4. (d) Repeat (a) on the degree-9 monomial design of Section 6.2.3 (no intercept, \lambda = 10^{-10}). Which of the three methods loses accuracy, and why?

Hint. For the SVD version, center the columns and the response first (the intercept is the mean of y minus the weights applied to the means of the columns). In (d) the reference is the SVD version.

Exercise 6.8 ★★ — Softmax regression from scratch. Implement the penalized cross-entropy loss and its gradient for K classes, with unpenalized intercepts: J = \frac1n\sum_i -\log p_{i,y_i} + \frac\lambda2\lVert\mathbf{W}\rVert_F^2. (a) Check your gradient against finite differences on random data. (b) Minimize J with scipy.optimize.minimize (method L-BFGS-B) on the standardized Iris data (3 classes, 4 features) for \lambda = 0.01, and compare the weights with those of LogisticRegression(C=1/(n*lam)). (c) Verify that \sum_k\mathbf{w}_k \approx \mathbf{0}, as in Exercise 6.5.

Hint. Store the parameters in one vector, theta = np.r_[W.ravel(), b]. With Y the one-hot matrix and P = softmax(Z @ W.T + b), the gradient is (P - Y).T @ Z / n + lam * W for \mathbf{W} and (P - Y).mean(axis=0) for \mathbf{b}. Use scipy.special.softmax or subtract the row maximum before exponentiating.

Exercise 6.9 ★★★ — Collinearity, measured. Take the standardized Diabetes data and add a constructed feature, a noisy copy of bmi: \text{bmi}_2 = \rho\,\text{bmi} + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\,\varepsilon with \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1) (this is a construction, to control \rho). For \rho = 0, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999: (a) compute the standard error of the coefficient of bmi from the formula \hat\sigma\sqrt{[(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}]_{jj}} and the VIF of bmi, and check that \mathrm{SE} = \hat\sigma\sqrt{\mathrm{VIF}/n} when the columns are standardized; (b) estimate the standard deviation of that coefficient by 300 bootstrap resamples and compare; (c) in the same bootstrap, compute the standard deviation of the sum of the two bmi coefficients and explain what it shows; (d) repeat (b) and (c) with ridge (\lambda = 10).

Hint. Draw \varepsilon once, with default_rng(SEED), reuse it for every \rho, and standardize the constructed column again. The VIF of column j is the j-th diagonal entry of the inverse of the correlation matrix of the columns. For the bootstrap, resample the rows with rng.integers(0, n, n).

Exercise 6.10 ★★★ — How does the best C depend on n? On the Breast Cancer data (malignant = 1), for training-set sizes n = 30, 60, 120, 240 and 30 random draws of the training set for each (the other patients form the test set): (a) choose C in \{10^{-3}, 10^{-2.5}, \dots, 10^3\} by 5-fold cross-validated log-loss on the training set; (b) also compute the oracle C, the one with the smallest test log-loss; (c) report, for each n, the median of both C’s and of the corresponding values \lambda = 1/(Cn), and the mean test log-loss of the CV-selected model, of the oracle, and of the unpenalized model (C=np.inf). Does the best \lambda decrease like 1/n, as the idea “a larger training set can afford a weaker penalty” suggests?

Hint. Use a pipeline (StandardScaler, LogisticRegression) and cross_val_predict(..., method="predict_proba") with StratifiedKFold. Skip draws in which the training set has fewer than 6 examples of a class. For n = 30 the unpenalized model may not converge: use max_iter=5000 and ignore the warnings (they are the separability of Section 6.4.4).

We now have two complete families of methods, the local one of Chapter 4 and the global, parametric one of this chapter, and a protocol to compare them. A recurring theme has been how the solution is computed: least squares has a closed form, but the logistic loss needs Newton’s method, whose step costs a d \times d linear solve and needs the Hessian. When d is large or n is huge, this is too expensive, and when the loss is not convex (as in neural networks) it is not even meaningful. Chapter 7 studies the alternative, first-order optimization: gradient descent, stochastic gradient descent, learning rates and conditioning, and shows why the singular values that governed ridge in this chapter also govern the speed of gradient descent.

The two other themes of the chapter will return. The logistic loss \log(1 + e^{-m}) is a smooth function of the margin m; Chapter 8 replaces it by the hinge loss \max(0, 1 - m) and obtains support vector machines, whose solution depends only on the examples near the boundary, and for which the margin bound of Section 3.8.4 is the natural guarantee. The dual form of ridge regression (Proposition 6.12) shows that the data enter only through inner products between examples; Chapter 9 exploits this observation to use feature maps of very high, even infinite, dimension without ever computing them: the kernel trick and the representer theorem. Chapter 10 replaces the \ell_2 penalty by the \ell_1 penalty, which sets coefficients exactly to zero and performs feature selection, and we shall see that doing the selection inside the cross-validation loop is essential. Chapter 11 returns to nonlinear models with decision trees and ensembles, whose probability estimates need the recalibration of Section 5.6.4.

A Hands-On Mathematical Guide with Jupyter Notebooks, scikit-learn and PyTorch

Mario Medone

Version 0.6.0 · 2026

Machine learning is built on ideas that every student of linear algebra and calculus already knows: vectors, matrices, projections, eigenvalues, gradients and the chain rule. This book shows how those ideas become working algorithms, starting from nearest neighbors and regularized least squares, passing through kernels, clustering and PCA, and arriving at deep networks, transformers and generative models.

Every chapter pairs mathematics with code. Derivations are written out step by step, every method is implemented in Python on real datasets taken from standard libraries, and each chapter closes with exercises of increasing difficulty, both by hand and on the computer. The chapters are Jupyter notebooks, so you can re-run every computation, change it, and see what happens.
This book is a work in progress and is published one chapter at a time. Each release has a version number, and version 1.0.0 will mark the complete book. The current version is 0.6.0.

Read online: 

https://​brosss98​.github​.io​/machine​-learning​-with​-python​-book/

Source code and notebooks: 

https://​github​.com​/Brosss98​/machine​-learning​-with​-python​-book

Report an error or suggest an improvement: 

https://​github​.com​/Brosss98​/machine​-learning​-with​-python​-book​/issues

The text of this book is licensed under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and the code under the MIT License. See 

Copyright and Editorial Information for the details.
This page collects the notation used throughout the book. Do not try to memorize it: each symbol is introduced again where it first appears, and you can return here whenever you need.

Symbol

Meaning

n

Number of samples (examples)

d

Number of features (input dimension)

K

Number of classes or clusters

\mathbf{x}_i\in\mathbb{R}^d

The i-th input vector

y_i

The label or target of the i-th example

\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}

Data matrix: its i-th row is \mathbf{x}_i^\top

\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}

Vector of all targets

S=\{(\mathbf{x}_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^{n}

Training set

In code, the data matrix is an array X of shape (n, d), with one sample per row, which is the convention of scikit-learn.

Symbol

Meaning

f

A prediction function; \hat{y}=f(\mathbf{x}) is the prediction for \mathbf{x}

\mathcal{H}

Hypothesis space: the set of functions a method can choose from

\mathbf{w},\ b

Weights and bias of a model

\boldsymbol{\theta}

Generic vector of parameters

\ell(y,\hat{y})

Loss on a single example

R(f)

Expected risk of f

\hat{R}_S(f)

Empirical risk of f on the training set S

\lambda

Regularization strength

\eta

Learning rate

\nabla_{\mathbf{w}} L

Gradient of the function L with respect to \mathbf{w}

\operatorname{argmin}_{\mathbf{w}}\, L(\mathbf{w})

The value of \mathbf{w} that minimizes L

Symbol

Meaning

f^\ast,\ R^\ast

Bayes predictor and Bayes risk: the smallest risk of any function

\eta(\mathbf{x})

Regression function \mathbb{E}[y \mid \mathbf{x}] (for y\in\{0,1\} it is \mathbb{P}(y=1\mid\mathbf{x})); not the learning rate

\hat f_S

The function chosen by empirical risk minimization on the training set S

f_{\mathcal{H}}

The best function in \mathcal{H}, that is, the one with the smallest expected risk

\varepsilon,\ \delta

Accuracy and failure probability of a guarantee: “with probability at least 1-\delta, the error is at most \varepsilon”

\Pi_{\mathcal{H}}(n)

Growth function: the largest number of labelings of n points that \mathcal{H} can produce

d_{\mathrm{VC}}

Vapnik–Chervonenkis dimension: the size of the largest set of points that \mathcal{H} can label in all possible ways

\hat{\mathfrak{R}}_S(\mathcal{F}),\ \mathfrak{R}_n(\mathcal{F})

Empirical and expected Rademacher complexity of a class \mathcal{F}

Symbol

Meaning

N_k(\mathbf{x})

The set of the k training points nearest to \mathbf{x} (its k nearest neighbors)

\hat f_k(\mathbf{x})

The prediction of the k-nearest-neighbor method at \mathbf{x}

f

The true regression function, f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbb{E}[y\mid\mathbf{x}] (the function called \eta in Chapter 3)

\sigma^2

Variance of the noise, y = f(\mathbf{x}) + \varepsilon

\text{bias}^2,\ \text{variance}

Squared systematic error and sensitivity to the training set of a prediction \hat f_S(\mathbf{x}_0): \mathbb{E}[(y_0-\hat f_S(\mathbf{x}_0))^2]=\sigma^2+\text{bias}^2+\text{variance}

Symbol

Meaning

K,\ \kappa(i)

Number of folds of cross-validation; the index of the fold that contains example i

\mathrm{CV}_K

The K-fold cross-validation estimate of the error: the average loss of each example under the model fitted without its fold

n_{\mathrm{val}},\ m

Size of a validation set; number of candidate models or configurations among which the best is selected

\mathrm{TP},\ \mathrm{FP},\ \mathrm{FN},\ \mathrm{TN}

Entries of the confusion matrix: true positives, false positives, false negatives, true negatives

\text{TPR}(t),\ \text{FPR}(t)

True-positive rate (recall) and false-positive rate of the rule “predict positive if the score is at least t”

S^+,\ S^-

Score of a randomly chosen positive and of a randomly chosen negative example

\text{AUC},\ \text{AP}

Area under the ROC curve; average precision (area under the precision–recall curve)

F_\beta

Weighted harmonic mean of precision and recall; \beta > 1 gives more weight to recall

\pi

Prevalence: the fraction of positive examples in the population

c_{FP},\ c_{FN},\ t^\ast

Costs of a false positive and of a false negative; the cost-optimal threshold t^\ast = c_{FP}/(c_{FP}+c_{FN}) for calibrated probabilities

h_{ii}

Leverage of example i in linear regression (diagonal of the hat matrix); the leave-one-out residual is e_i/(1-h_{ii})

Symbol

Meaning

\lambda,\ \hat{\mathbf{w}}_\lambda

Strength of the \ell_2 penalty and the ridge estimator, which minimizes \lVert\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{X}\mathbf{w}\rVert^2+\lambda\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2 (alpha in scikit-learn’s Ridge); for logistic regression the objective is the mean loss plus \tfrac\lambda2\lVert\mathbf{w}\rVert^2. The intercept is never penalized

\sigma_j,\ \mathbf{u}_j,\ \mathbf{v}_j,\ f_j(\lambda)

Singular values and left and right singular vectors of the centered feature matrix; shrinkage factors f_j(\lambda)=\sigma_j^2/(\sigma_j^2+\lambda) of ridge. (Do not confuse \sigma_j with \sigma^2, the noise variance, nor with \sigma(\cdot), the sigmoid)

\mathbf{H}_\lambda,\ \mathrm{df}(\lambda)

Smoother (hat) matrix of ridge, \hat{\mathbf{y}}=\mathbf{H}_\lambda\mathbf{y}, and effective degrees of freedom \mathrm{df}(\lambda)=\operatorname{tr}\mathbf{H}_\lambda=\sum_jf_j(\lambda) (plus 1 for the intercept)

\mathrm{VIF}_j

Variance inflation factor of feature j, 1/(1-R_j^2) with R_j^2 the R^2 of regressing feature j on the others

\sigma(z)

Logistic function (sigmoid) 1/(1+e^{-z}); the log-odds \log\frac{\eta}{1-\eta} are linear in the features

\tilde{\mathbf{X}},\ \boldsymbol\theta

Design matrix with a column of ones in front, and the parameter vector (b,\mathbf{w}) that includes the intercept

p_i,\ \mathbf{S}

Predicted probability of class 1 for example i; the diagonal matrix \mathbf{S}=\mathrm{diag}\big(p_i(1-p_i)\big) of the Newton weights. (Elsewhere in the chapter p is the number of parameters)

m_i,\ L,\ J_\lambda

Signed score m_i=(2y_i-1)z_i; negative log-likelihood (log-loss, cross-entropy) L=\sum_i\log(1+e^{-m_i}); penalized objective J_\lambda

C

Inverse regularization strength of scikit-learn: C multiplies the sum of the losses, so \lambda=1/(Cn)

K,\ p_k(\mathbf{x}),\ \mathbf{w}_k,\ b_k

In softmax regression, K is the number of classes (in Chapter 5 it is the number of folds), the probability of class k and the weights and intercept of its score

\boldsymbol\varphi(\mathbf{x})

Feature map: a fixed function from \mathbb{R}^d to \mathbb{R}^p (for example all monomials up to a given degree); models linear in \boldsymbol\varphi are nonlinear in \mathbf{x}

Symbol

Meaning

\mathcal{D}

The unknown distribution that generates the data

\mathbb{P}(A)

Probability of the event A

\mathbb{E}[X],\ \operatorname{Var}(X)

Expectation and variance of a random variable

\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)

Gaussian distribution with mean \mu and variance \sigma^2

\mathbb{I}[\cdot]

Indicator function: equal to 1 if the condition holds and 0 otherwise

Vectors are columns. A vector \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^d is a d\times 1 column, and \mathbf{x}^\top is a row.

Indices start at 1 in the mathematics and at 0 in Python. The first sample is \mathbf{x}_1 in the formulas and X[0] in the code. This is a frequent source of off-by-one mistakes.

Code is written in monospace. Names such as X, y, and w match the symbols in the text whenever possible.

Local notation. A chapter may introduce extra symbols for its own purposes. They are defined where they are first used.

Machine learning is usually taught in one of two ways. In the first, it is a collection of recipes: import a model, call fit, call predict, and hope for the best. In the second, it is an abstract theory in which the connection with practice is hard to see. This book sits between the two. It assumes that you already know linear algebra and calculus, and it uses them as the language in which machine learning is explained and then checks every statement with code.

For a reader with that background, most of machine learning is less foreign than it first appears. Ridge regression is a linear system with one small modification. Principal component analysis is the singular value decomposition applied to centered data. Training a neural network is the chain rule applied systematically to a long composition of functions. The aim of this book is to make such connections explicit, to explain the intuition behind each formula, and to let you verify the result on a computer.

The book is written for university students who are starting out in machine learning. It assumes:

Linear algebra: vectors, matrices, dot products, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and the singular value decomposition.

Calculus: derivatives, partial derivatives, gradients, and the chain rule.

No previous knowledge of machine learning is required. Some familiarity with programming helps. Chapter 2 reviews the Python tools used throughout the book (NumPy, pandas, and matplotlib) together with the small amount of probability that the later chapters need. Advanced mathematics, such as measure theory, is not required, and proofs are given only when they help to build intuition.

Every technical chapter is built around the same ingredients:

Learning objectives and intuition, so that you know where the chapter is going and why.

Mathematical formulation and derivations, written step by step in a way that explains each manipulation.

Figures generated by Python code that you can run and modify.

Hands-on implementation on real datasets from standard libraries such as scikit-learn, seaborn, and torchvision.

Worked examples solved both by hand and in code, so that the two can be compared.

Exercises of increasing difficulty, divided into manual (analytical) exercises and Python (computational) exercises. They are meant to be challenging but accessible.

The book follows a practice-first approach. Concepts are introduced together with the code that implements them, and the datasets are real ones. Each chapter is a Jupyter notebook, so you can execute it from beginning to end on your own computer.

The book is organized in five parts.

Part I, Foundations (Chapters 1–3). What machine learning is, how to set up your environment, the Python and probability tools used throughout, and statistical learning theory, the framework that tells us what it means for a model to learn and to generalize.

Part II, Classical Supervised Learning (Chapters 4–11). Nearest-neighbor methods and the bias–variance trade-off, cross-validation and hyperparameter tuning, regularized least squares and logistic regression, stochastic gradient descent, support vector machines, kernels and the representer theorem, sparsity and feature selection (OMP, Lasso, Elastic Net), and decision trees and ensembles.

Part III, Unsupervised Learning (Chapters 12–13). Clustering (k-means, vector quantization, spectral clustering, and how to choose the number of clusters), and dimensionality reduction with SVD, PCA, and kernel PCA.

Part IV, Deep Learning (Chapters 14–21). Neural network fundamentals, backpropagation and the practice of training deep networks, convolutional networks and their applications, recurrent networks (RNN, LSTM, GRU), attention and transformers, autoencoders and GANs, and graph neural networks.

Part V, Decisions and Modern AI (Chapters 22–23). Reinforcement learning with Markov decision processes, Monte Carlo methods, and temporal-difference learning, followed by large language models, modern architectures, AI agents, and future directions.

The book closes with conclusions, appendices (a math cheat sheet, a Python cheat sheet, solutions to the exercises, and a glossary), and a bibliography.

If you are following a full course, read the chapters in order: each one builds on the previous ones. If your main interest is deep learning, a faster route is to read Chapters 1–3 and 5–7, which introduce the setup, the learning framework, evaluation, linear models, and gradient-based optimization, and then to move to Part IV, returning to the classical methods later. In either case, do the exercises: the notebooks are designed to be changed and re-run, and that is where most of the learning happens.

The book aims to be mathematically honest without being heavy. When a result is stated without proof, the text says so and indicates where to find the proof, and the bibliography collects references for readers who want to go further. When a simplification is made for the sake of clarity, it is flagged as such.

This book would not exist without the open-source community. The code is written in Python and runs in Jupyter notebooks. The book is built with Jupyter Book, a project of the Executable Books community. The numerical and learning code relies on NumPy, SciPy, pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, scikit-learn, and PyTorch, including its torchvision and torchaudio libraries. Thanks go to the maintainers and contributors of all these projects, and to the researchers and institutions who created and released the open datasets used in the examples; each dataset is cited where it appears.
